newsitem.title: UK: Moody's sees foreign currency EMU ceilings at AAA.
newsitem.headline: Moody's sees foreign currency EMU ceilings at AAA.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday that it expected the foreign currency debt rating ceilings for countries joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be triple-A.

Moody's said that as a result of the changed rating structure, public and private entities in EMU countries would have a Aaa ceiling and would no longer be constrained by any local ceilings below that top notch.
"This would probably have a beneficial effect on asset-backed securities," Moody's said.
"Under EMU, any issuer can get a credit rating based on its own credit analysis," said David Levey, co-head of Moody's sovereign risk unit, speaking at a presentation on the report.
Levey said British sovereign ratings were unlikely to be affected if the country stayed out of EMU.
"I don't think there's any chance that the UK...will be affected even if stays outside of EMU," Levey said.
Britain currently has Aaa sovereign ratings from Moody's for both its foreign currency and local currency debt.
The Moody's report follows similar reports from rival rating agencies Standard & Poor's and IBCA last year on the subject of EMU.

The euro's introduction and its implications for credit risk in European countries have been a subject of research in recent months. Speculation about the effects of EMU has been a big topic for financial markets as the launch date draws nearer.
Levey said several of Moody's recent sovereign rating actions had already incorporated the credit implications of EMU.

"For example, earlier this month Moody's upgraded the foreign currency ceiling of Ireland to Aa1 and confirmed the Irish government's Aaa local currency debt rating to reflect its assessment that the approach of EMU increases the likelihood of continued fiscal discipline and low inflation," Moody's said.

Explaining the rationale for the government bond ratings, Levey said, "We expect that EMU-bloc governments will benefit from the broadening of the European capital market because investors will no longer be concerned with foreign exchange risk within the bloc."
But he added, "For some governments joining EMU, the benefits associated with the loss of foreign exchange risk may be outweighed by the loss of prime creditor status within their own countries."
When the foreign risk disappears, lenders (investors) will no longer have a clear preference for bonds of their own governments and an important financial safety net will be weakened, Levey said.
One technical point that Moody's made was that the redenomination of outstanding domestic currency debt into euro debt would not be regarded as "an event of default".
